full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.:- In this appeal by special leave the principal question is whether the decision of the lower Appellate Court, as confirmed in second appeal by the High Court Division, that the holding in question was abandoned by its owner-tenant Priyabala and the plaintiffs-landlords took khas possession thereof under section 87 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. is based on proper consideration of the evidence on record. 

 2. The impugned order of the High Court Division is dated 1 June 1983 and the matter arises from O.C, Suit No. 83 of 1963 of the Court of Munsif, Rajshahi. For the purpose of disposal of this appeal history of the suit land need not be traced beyond the admitted raiyat Priyabala, who got it by settlement from the landlords, Sudhir and Bejoy, in 1342 B.S. corresponding to 1935 A.D. Superior interest of the holding was thereafter acquired by the plaintiffs-respondents by a Deed of Exchange with their properties in West Bengal whereupon Priyabala accepted the plaintiff as her landlords and paid rent to them in 1953. Thereafter, controversy started. According to the plaintiffs, Priyabala left for West Bengal for good and abandoned the holding without making any arrangement either for cultivation of the land or for payment of the rent and consequently the plaintiffs by serving a notice under section 87 of the Bengal Tenancy Act entered upon the land and took khas possession: But defendants Nos. 1 and 2 wives of defendant No. 6 on the basis of a spurious claim of settlement from Priyabala threatened to dispossess the plaintiffs who then filed the suit for declaration of title, confirmation of possession, in the alternative for recovery of possession. During the pendency of the suit, defendants No.1 and 2 transferred the land to defendant Nos.3 and 4 without Court's permission. 

 6. The question of abandonment of the holding is found to have been elaborately discussed in the judgments of both the trial Court and the lower Appellate Court. It has been found by both the Courts that Priyabala left the then Pakistan and started residing in West Bengal from where she never returned to Pakistan nor did she make any arrangement for payment of the rent. As to cultivation of the land, defendant No. 5 a former bargader of Priyabala claimed to be cultivating it on behalf of the owner Priyabala, but when Priyabala did not return to the country nor paid any rent, the bargadars, claim of possession on behalf of the owner fell through. He resisted the plaintiffs possession for a time and the plaintiffs unsuccessfully brought a. criminal proceeding against him under section 144 Cr.P.C. It is at this stage that defendants Nos. 1 and 2 appeared on the scene and claimed possession on the basis of the spurious settlement whereupon the plaintiffs again filed a proceeding against them all under section 144 Cr.P.C and got a favourable order. Filing of these proceedings, which are quasi judicial in nature, simply shows that the petitioners claim was sought to be thwarted in the absence of Priyabala by mere trespassers. The lower Appellate Court on consideration of these facts and circumstances; particularly non-payment of rent by or on behalf of Priyabala ever since she left Pakistan, came to a clear finding that Priyabala abandoned her holding whereupon the plaintiffs entered upon the land by serving a notice under section 87 of the B T. Act. Mr. T.H. Khan contends that the plaintiffs' claim as to abandonment of the holding fell through when the Collector dropped the proceeding under section 87 of the B.T. Act. But it should be noted that the Collector got hardly anything to do in the matter except causing a notice under section 87 "published in the prescribed manner". The landlords' right to enter upon the holding under section 87(1) does not depend upon Collector's discretion. But if the landlord enters upon the holding by serving a notice, the raiyat may file a suit for recovery of possession of the land at any time not later than expiration of two years from the date of publication of the notice. In this case, Priyabala the riyat did not file any such suit as she did never return from India. In the circumstances the learned Single Judge of the High Court rightly refused to disturb the finding is to abandonment. We find this decision to be well-founded both in law and fact leaving no scope for interference. The appeal is dismissed without any order as to costs.
